slides.title: Best-First Search, A*, and Heuristic Quality
slides.visibleText:
DRIVING QUESTION
What deserves to leave the frontier next?

Retrieve four ideas: OPEN, CLOSED, path cost g(n), and parent links. Today a heuristic h(n) changes the expansion order.

GREEDY BEST-FIRST

Select the frontier node with minimum predicted remaining cost h(n).

A*

Select the frontier node with minimum estimated total cost g(n)+h(n).

HEURISTIC QUALITY

Ask what h guarantees, how much search it saves, and what it costs to compute.

slides.title: Follow the smallest estimated distance to the goal
slides.visibleText:
SELECTION RULE
Choose min h(n) from OPEN

The heuristic estimates cost from n to a goal. Greedy best-first uses that estimate alone, so “looks closest” is not the same as “lies on a least-cost path.”

OPEN · PRIORITY QUEUE

Stores generated but unexpanded nodes, keyed here by h(n).

CLOSED · EXPLORED RECORD

Records expanded states and supports duplicate detection.

PARENTS AND BEST G

Recover a path and decide whether a newly found duplicate is better.

GUARANTEE CHECK
Greedy best-first is neither generally optimal nor complete in unrestricted spaces. OPEN and CLOSED organize work; they do not create a shortest-path guarantee.

slides.title: Generate broadly, then select the most promising frontier node
slides.visibleText:
Put the start node in OPEN; keep CLOSED empty.
Remove a node with minimum h from OPEN.
Test whether its state satisfies the goal.
Expand it and evaluate each successor.
Insert unseen successors; update a duplicate when the new record is better.
Record the expanded state in CLOSED and repeat.
“Backtrack” means choose the next-best OPEN entry

Unlike hill climbing, the algorithm keeps alternatives. A dead end does not force it to undo physical actions; it simply pops another frontier entry.

PATH RECOVERY
Store a parent pointer with each accepted record. When a goal is selected, follow parents back to the start and reverse the chain.

slides.title: The pseudocode needs explicit duplicate and path policy
slides.visibleText:
Procedure for maintaining the frontier, explored record, and current path.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
Read the data structures, then repair the contract

OPEN is a min-priority queue keyed by h. CLOSED records expanded states. Each accepted node stores its state, parent, g value, and h value.

DUPLICATE POLICY
If a successor is unseen, insert it. If it represents a known state through a better g, update its record and parent; whether a CLOSED state must reopen depends on the algorithm and heuristic conditions.
CORRECTED GUARANTEE
Following parent links returns the path the search found. Greedy best-first does not guarantee that this path is shortest.

slides.title: An admissible heuristic never overestimates remaining optimal cost
slides.visibleText:
The intended idea is a lower bound on true optimal remaining cost.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
TRUE REMAINING COST

h*(n) is the cost of an optimal path from n to a goal.

ADMISSIBILITY

0 ≤ h(n) ≤ h*(n) for every n, with h(goal)=0.

A* SELECTION

f(n)=g(n)+h(n); admissibility belongs to h, not to greedy selection.

OPTIMALITY CONDITIONS
Tree-search A* is optimal with an admissible h under standard nonnegative-cost and termination assumptions. Graph-search A* additionally needs consistency or a correct reopen policy.

slides.title: Three questions expose three common confusions
slides.visibleText:
Q1 · Perfect?
Q2 · 8-puzzle
Q3 · “BFS”
ASK

Must an admissible heuristic predict the exact remaining cost?

ANSWER

No. It may underestimate. The requirement is 0 ≤ h(n) ≤ h*(n), not h(n)=h*(n). A more accurate admissible heuristic usually saves more search.

PROVE

State the relevant inequality or cost assumption. A familiar name is not a proof of admissibility.

actions.label: Open the eight-puzzle admissibility question
actions.stateText: Q1 · Perfect? Q2 · 8-puzzle Q3 · “BFS” ASK Which familiar 8-puzzle heuristics are admissible? ANSWER Misplaced tiles and Manhattan distance. With unit-cost legal moves, each misplaced tile needs at least one move and each tile must travel at least its Manhattan distance. Any third heuristic must be proved pointwise: if h3(n)>h*(n) anywhere, it is not admissible. PROVE State the relevant inequality or cost assumption. A familiar name is not a proof of admissibility.

actions.label: Open the BFS abbreviation question
actions.stateText: Q1 · Perfect? Q2 · 8-puzzle Q3 · “BFS” ASK Is “BFS” the same algorithm as A*? ANSWER The abbreviation is too ambiguous. Breadth-first search matches uniform-cost search, and therefore A* with h=0, when every action has the same positive cost (often normalized to one). Greedy best-first search orders by h alone and is not A*. PROVE State the relevant inequality or cost assumption. A familiar name is not a proof of admissibility.

slides.title: Estimate the total solution cost through each frontier node
slides.visibleText:
A* SELECTION RULE
Choose min f(n)=g(n)+h(n)

g is cost already paid from the start. h estimates optimal cost remaining to a goal. Their sum estimates the cost of a complete solution constrained to pass through n.

G(N) · KNOWN SO FAR

Computed from the accepted parent path and edge costs.

H(N) · PREDICTED REMAINDER

Problem knowledge that should be cheaper than solving the remainder exactly.

F(N) · ESTIMATED TOTAL

The key used by A*’s minimum priority queue.

slides.title: Equal depth is not the same as equal estimated total cost
slides.visibleText:
The two methods impose different frontier priorities.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
Name the assumptions behind each guarantee

Breadth-first search is complete with finite branching and is optimal when every action has the same cost. A* can handle unequal nonnegative costs when its heuristic and graph policy satisfy the required conditions.

EQUIVALENCE CONDITION
A* with h=0 orders by g, which is uniform-cost search. Depth and g induce the same ordering when every step has the same positive cost, often normalized to one.

slides.title: A lower-bound geography heuristic focuses a national route
slides.visibleText:
A* searches a rail network from Washington, D.C. to Los Angeles.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
Srossd · Own work · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons curid=35900474
Replay animation
Great-circle distance is a useful lower bound

Rail distance already traveled supplies g. Great-circle distance to Los Angeles supplies h because a rail route cannot be shorter than the direct surface distance between its endpoints.

ASSUMPTION
The comparison is valid only when edge costs and h use compatible units and the route cost cannot undercut direct distance.

slides.title: Set h(n)=0 and A* becomes uniform-cost search
slides.visibleText:
With h=0, the frontier is ordered entirely by accumulated path cost g.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
Ibmua · Work by uploader · Public Domain · Wikimedia Commons curid=6282617
Replay animation
f(n)=g(n)+0=g(n)

On a graph with nonnegative edge costs, this is uniform-cost/Dijkstra-style search: expand the unsettled node with minimum known distance from the start.

DO NOT OVERGENERALIZE
Breadth-first search is equivalent only when the same positive step cost makes shallowest depth and smallest g the same ordering.

slides.title: A consistent heuristic obeys a triangle inequality on every edge
slides.visibleText:
Consistency compares the estimate at a node with one step plus the estimate at its successor.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
EDGE CONDITION

h(n) ≤ c(n,n′)+h(n′) for every successor n′, with h(goal)=0.

MONOTONE F

Along a path, consistency makes f(n′) ≥ f(n).

CONSEQUENCE

Under standard conditions, consistency implies admissibility and lets graph-search A* close a node at its best g.

DIAGNOSTIC
Check one edge at a time. A violation means a later path may improve a state that was already expanded.

slides.title: An inconsistent heuristic can force a CLOSED node to reopen
slides.visibleText:
ADMISSIBLE BUT INCONSISTENT HEURISTIC · 1 OF 6
Initialize S

Start with S. Its true optimal cost is 4 and h(S)=3.

Previous
Next
Reset
Graph and heuristic
S—3→A · S—1→B · B—1→A · A—2→G
h(S)=3, h(B)=3, h(A)=0, h(G)=0. Every h is admissible.
OPEN
[S: g0, f3]
CLOSED
[]
Consistency fails on B→A: 3 > 1+0. A better g must reopen A.

slides.title: A more informed admissible heuristic gives tighter lower bounds
slides.visibleText:
Pointwise larger admissible values supply tighter lower bounds.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
DOMINANCE

If admissible h1 and h2 satisfy h1(n) ≤ h2(n) for all n, h2 dominates h1.

8-PUZZLE EXAMPLE

Manhattan distance dominates misplaced-tile count for the standard unit-cost puzzle.

SEARCH EFFECT

With comparable tie-breaking, A* using h2 typically expands no more nodes than A* using h1.

ENGINEERING QUALIFICATION
“More informed” does not mean free. Count the time and memory needed to compute or retrieve the stronger heuristic.

slides.title: Search savings must exceed the cost of control knowledge
slides.visibleText:
Total problem-solving cost can be U-shaped as heuristic effort increases.
CLICK IMAGE TO ENLARGE
Optimize total cost, not node count alone

A stronger heuristic can reduce search and rule-application cost, yet require more preprocessing, memory, sensing, or computation at every node.

MEASURE
Total effort = search work + heuristic/control work. The most informed available heuristic is not automatically the fastest end-to-end system.

slides.title: Use one lens for h and another for the search algorithm
slides.visibleText:
01
Heuristic function h
Judge an estimate

Admissibility
0 ≤ h(n) ≤ h*(n)
Never overestimates true remaining cost.

Consistency
h(n) ≤ c(n,n′)+h(n′)
Also monotonicity or local admissibility.

Informedness
h1(n) ≤ h2(n) ≤ h*(n)
h2 is the tighter admissible lower bound.

02
Search algorithm
Judge the whole procedure

Complete?
Finds a solution if one exists.

Optimal?
Returns a least-cost solution.

Time?
How much work grows?

Space?
How much must be stored?

Algorithm admissibility is the classical synonym for an optimality guarantee—not heuristic admissibility.
Is h1 admissible?
Is h2 consistent?
Is DFS consistent?
Is best-first search complete?
Is algorithm A admissible?
HEURISTIC h
Is h1 admissible?

Check 0 ≤ h1(n) ≤ h*(n) for every state.

slides.title: Offline deterministic search is only one corner of agency
slides.visibleText:
1
Physical action

Backing up may be costly or impossible; computational backtracking is not physical reversal.

2
Uncertainty

Partial observations, stochastic outcomes, and unknown models break a fixed deterministic graph.

3
Change

Dynamic worlds require online sensing, replanning, or policies rather than one offline path.

4
Other agents

Cooperation changes coordination; competition requires adversarial reasoning.

ENVIRONMENT AUDIT

Deterministic, stochastic, or nondeterministic?

Fully observable, partially observable, or unknown?

Episodic or sequential; static or dynamic?

Discrete or continuous; known or learned?

Single-agent, cooperative, or competitive?

slides.title: Trace it, justify it, and decide when it belongs
slides.visibleText:
1 · TRACE
Execute the frontier

Given a weighted graph and h table, show every OPEN, CLOSED, parent, g, and f update—including a reopened state.

2 · JUSTIFY
Prove the heuristic claim

Use 0≤h≤h* for admissibility and h(n)≤c+h(n′) for consistency. State all cost and termination assumptions.

3 · DECIDE
Defend the model

Choose greedy best-first, A*, uniform-cost, breadth-first, or a non-path-search model—and name the guarantee and tradeoff.

Reading and bibliography

Read George F. Luger, Artificial Intelligence: Structures and Strategies for Complex Problem Solving, 6th ed., Chapter 4 (Addison-Wesley, 2009); and review Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 3rd ed., Chapter 3 (Prentice Hall, 2010).
